title: Oura, HealthKit and Menopause Data: Leave Room for the Person | Terra
summary: Oura’s MIS and Apple’s HealthKit menopause APIs bring different kinds of data together. The useful details are in the answers, dates and missing entries.
body_markdown:
## An unusually consequential` .none`


Apple’s` HKCategoryTypeIdentifier.menopausalState` is available from iOS 27.0 and watchOS 27.0, among other platforms. Its values come from` HKCategoryValueMenopausalState` :` .perimenopause` ,` .menopause` and` .none` . Each sample is a dated entry, with identical start and end dates. HealthKit rejects attempts to save it as an interval.


The interesting bit is` .none` . It means the person explicitly confirmed that neither menopause nor perimenopause applied at the recorded date. It doesn't mean unknown, unset or missing. This is a pleasing amount of care to put into an enum. A confirmed answer and an absence of information stay distinguishable, provided the app doesn't undo the distinction with a default value.


Apple’s recording and querying guide leaves the interpretation of a timeline to the app. An entry dated September 10 records the state at that date. Extending it forward to fill a month on a chart is an interpretation. The resulting shaded area can be useful, but it should remain traceable to the entry that produced it. Otherwise a reasonable display choice starts looking like a much more complete history than anyone supplied.


Apple also suggests an order for presenting conflicting entries on the same date: menopause, then perimenopause, then none. We'd keep the underlying sources visible even when following that priority. Resolving the display doesn't resolve the disagreement, and a recorded user report shouldn't acquire the appearance of a clinician-confirmed diagnosis along the way. A correction needs to flow through to the derived view, too.


The separate` bleedingAfterMenopause` type does represent an interval and uses` HKCategoryValueVaginalBleeding` for intensity. It also has iOS 27.0 and watchOS 27.0 availability. That distinction from both state entries and menstrual flow needs to survive the journey into your database, even if one generic “reproductive health event” table looks convenient.


## The questionnaire and the ring keep different hours


Putting the data on one screen is appealing. Putting it all under one date is where things start going wrong.


An MIS assessment completed on September 18 refers to the preceding fortnight. A state entry made that day concerns a particular date. Last night's wearable observations cover their own period. Showing all three under “September 18” without those qualifications asks the reader to supply quite a lot of missing context.


The sensor data has detail worth keeping, too. Oura describes its temperature measure as average nighttime skin-temperature change relative to a personal baseline, distinct from basal or core temperature. Its daily value and smoothed trend view use different windows. “Temperature” on its own is an ambitious column name for all of that.


The same caution applies to familiar measurements such as sleep. Our[Apple Watch and Oura sleep-stage comparison](https://tryterra.co/blog/apple-vs-oura-sleep-stage-comparisons-94f359368e0a) is a useful reminder that matching labels can still conceal different observations.


A useful comparison would align observations with the assessment’s recall period while still showing when the assessment was completed. If there are eight nights of sleep data in that fortnight, the missing nights belong in the view. The measurement period, units, baseline relationship and source also belong with each wearable value. Local dates and timezone offsets matter when the thing being recorded is a night that crosses midnight.


There is no requirement for the results to agree. Someone can report less disruption while their recorded menopausal state remains unchanged. A wearable series may show little movement while symptoms are affecting everyday life. These combinations are worth discussing, rather than smoothing into a composite number that is easier to lay out. Nor does movement in two series establish a cause, or a temperature deviation alone establish menopause.


## Let the person decide what follows them


HealthKit permissions are separate for each data type and for reading and writing. Apple deliberately hides read denial from the app: a query can look as though there is no data. That makes “No entries available to this app” a considerably better description than “Not in menopause.” The wording is less definitive because the app knows less.


For a questionnaire collected directly by your app, you can distinguish not started, partly completed and submitted. For a wearable connection, you may know that syncing failed. An otherwise empty period can stay unexplained; there's no need to assign it a reason the data doesn't provide. A visible gap is useful information about the record's limits.


Apple’s recording guide supports read-only access when an app only needs to display existing state entries. Sharing information onward is another decision: Apple requires express permission for disclosure to third parties, subject to its sharing rules. And people can change permissions or delete records outside your app, so a summary can't remain confidently current while ignoring those changes.


For the wearable part of that view, Terra brings[Oura data](https://tryterra.co/integrations/oura) and[Apple Health through the iOS SDK](https://docs.tryterra.co/reference/health-and-fitness-api/sdk-references/ios-swift) into the same delivery format. The[standardisation layer](https://tryterra.co/blog/behind-the-scenes-the-data-standardisation-process-60f6636440eb) saves you from building separate importers for a ring and a watch, while the source and meaning of their observations still belong in the view. Confirm the supported types, exact field mappings and permissions for the SDK version you plan to ship; MIS partner access and Apple’s new menopause types need their own availability checks.


The care-team view we'd want is fairly modest: the person's assessment, its period and source, the dated state entry, and the wearable observations actually available. A clinician's annotation can sit alongside them with its own provenance. There is something reassuring about a screen that leaves room for an unfinished answer or a disagreement. It gives the person a way to explain what the data hasn't captured, and gives the care team a clearer place to listen.


There is more useful product work in making that conversation easier than in maintaining another wearable parser. A shared Terra integration leaves room for the person’s account to remain the part you design around.
